messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun, a 36-year-old detective, had always defined himself by his composure and resilience. He was the man who ran towards chaos, who could compartmentalise the grim realities of his job and return home to his wife, Priya, as a steadfast partner. This carefully constructed identity began to fracture six months ago, after a case involving child neglect dredged up memories he had long suppressed. The trauma was not from the streets he policed, but from the sterile silence of his childhood home. For a year, when he was eight, he had lived with an aunt whose discipline was cold and methodical. Punishment meant being locked in a small, unheated bathroom for hours. He can still recall the specific, biting cold of the tile floor seeping into his skin, the final, booming slam of the wooden door, and the profound terror of being utterly alone in the dark.

These sensory fragments now intrude upon his present. A door slamming down the hall at the precinct can make his heart hammer against his ribs, his focus shattering into a million pieces. In these moments, his reaction feels like more than just a startle; it feels like a profound personal failure. The sudden, uncontrollable surge of panic convinces him that his reactions prove he is a lousy coper. A man in his line of work, he tells himself, should be made of sterner stuff. This isn't just a symptom; it's evidence that there is something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, a deep, internal defect that has been there all along.

This corrosive belief that he is weak and broken has reshaped his life. Certain that his colleagues can see the flaw in him, that his incompetence is written all over his face, Arjun began to systematically withdraw. He stopped going to the canteen, taking his lunch at his desk to avoid the chatter and the risk of being seen as ‘off’. This growing isolation feeds his sense that he doesn't know himself anymore; the confident, decisive man he once was feels like a stranger whose memory is fading. To manage this feeling of being an imposter, he started avoiding going out entirely, making excuses to Priya about paperwork when friends invited them over, preferring the controlled quiet of his home to the unpredictability of the world.

His strategies, however, have only tightened the trap. The more he avoids people, the more his world shrinks, and the more his isolation confirms his belief that he is defective. A capable man, a good husband, wouldn't hide like this. This self-recrimination is loudest at night. He dreads the moment Priya falls asleep, leaving him alone in the quiet house. To postpone the inevitable, he delays sleep, staying up until the early hours watching old movies on the sofa until he passes out from sheer exhaustion. This chronic sleep deprivation has frayed his nerves raw, leaving him even more susceptible to his triggers. The exhaustion makes him jumpier, and the sound of a car door slamming on the street outside now feels as loud and immediate as the one from his childhood.

Convinced of his own fragility, his mind is now in a constant state of high alert. He finds himself scanning rooms, anticipating the slam of a door, tensing up when the air conditioning creates a cool draft on his skin. This hypervigilance, born from the belief that he is no longer able to cope with the world, makes it far more likely that he will encounter a trigger. The cold tile of his own bathroom floor against his bare feet in the morning is no longer a neutral sensation; it’s a direct line to the past, capable of derailing his entire day. His home, once a sanctuary, now feels mined with sensory threats he is powerless to avoid.

The breaking point came during a stakeout. He was assigned an overnight shift in an unfamiliar, empty apartment. The thought of sleeping alone in that strange place, with its creaks and unfamiliar sounds, was unbearable. He called in sick, a lie that felt heavy and shameful, leaving his partner to cover the shift alone. The professional failure was acute, a stark confirmation of his worthlessness. When Priya found him the next morning, still on the sofa, hollow-eyed and unshaven, she told him, "I don't know who you are anymore." Hearing his deepest fear of identity loss echoed in her voice was what finally propelled him to seek help. Arjun comes to therapy not just to quiet the ghosts of the past, but with the desperate, fragile hope of finding the man he once was, the man he is terrified is gone for good.
